extracted.intended_audience: researchers and organizations evaluating Lean/Mathlib for formal mathematics, verification, or industry use
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for assessing Mathlib as a foundation for formal mathematics research and verification, aimed at decision-makers, researchers, and engineers considering Lean/Mathlib for projects or organizational adoption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breadth of coverage / comprehensiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathlib's breadth of coverage spans core mathematics fundamentals including abstract algebra, analysis, combinatorics, dynamics, geometry, linear algebra, probability and number theory, and ... extends into computer science foundations with formalized data structures, logic, computability, and complexity theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the mathematics relevant to your domain is already formalized; review the Mathlib community library overview or Mathlib documentation to determine coverage. Presence of core and domain-specific formalizations reduces effort to adopt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design principles: abstraction, generality, composability
rubrics_metrics.description: The library follows rigorous design principles that prioritize abstraction, generality, and composability—qualities that are essential for both research mathematics and industry applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer libraries whose design emphasizes reusable, abstract, and composable components so different projects can build on shared foundations. Avoid ad-hoc or overly-specialized definitions that hinder reuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reusability and enablement of collaboration
rubrics_metrics.description: By providing a common foundation of formalized mathematics emphasizing reusability and composability, Mathlib enables collaboration between researchers who may be working on different parts of a complex mathematical theory, and permits new collaborators to easily build on prior work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how well the library's structure allows multiple contributors to interoperate and extend proofs or definitions without duplication. Look for examples of cross-project reuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Code quality and human review process
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathlib maintains high standards for code quality. A human expert reviews each contribution before it is accepted, and only the strongest approach to any given topic is included. Maintaining the cohesiveness of the library as a whole is a key goal of the review process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check contribution review policies and examples of review decisions. A rigorous human review process that favors strong, cohesive approaches indicates higher long-term maintainability; beware projects without consistent review standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sustainable maintenance and institutional support
rubrics_metrics.description: The Mathlib Initiative is a strategic program ... established to ensure the long-term continuity of Mathlib as a high-quality library. By providing professional infrastructure for the library and its downstream users, the Mathlib Initiative addresses the scaling challenges that come with a rapidly growing ecosystem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a library has formal maintenance programs, funding, or institutional support to ensure continuity and professional infrastructure for large-scale use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automated quality assurance tooling (linters)
rubrics_metrics.description: Automated linters check for common mistakes in definitions, type class instances, and simplification lemmas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confirm availability and coverage of static-analysis tools that detect common formalization mistakes. Such tooling helps scale contributions and keeps library quality consistent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuous integration for compatibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Continuous integration ensures that new contributions maintain compatibility with existing code.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require CI that runs full or targeted checks on changes to prevent regressions. A CI system that verifies compatibility across the codebase signals robustness for large projects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic documentation infrastructure
rubrics_metrics.description: Systematic documentation infrastructure ensures the library is maintainable and enables effective collaboration across the research community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate documentation depth (API docs, tutorials, examples) and whether documentation is kept in sync with code. Good docs lower onboarding cost and reduce misuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scalability of tooling and process
rubrics_metrics.description: These tools have helped Mathlib scale to over two million lines of code while maintaining high quality standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the combination of human review, linters, CI, and documentation has demonstrable ability to scale to large codebases; scalability reduces risk for large organizational adoption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proven industry and research applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathlib's comprehensive coverage has made it valuable for industry applications including cryptography and software verification. Examples: AWS's SampCert, multiple zkEVM project tracks, Starkware’s Cairo verification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for real-world projects and case studies that have successfully used the library; these serve as evidence of practicality and maturity for production use-cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability for AI and automated theorem proving
rubrics_metrics.description: Integration of artificial intelligence with Lean and Mathlib represents one of the most exciting developments ... Google DeepMind's AlphaProof achieving silver medal performance at IMO 2024 by training on Mathlib, and Project Numina building on Mathlib as foundation for AI.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If automated proof search or ML-assisted proving is important, evaluate whether the library's scale and structure support training and inference for theorem-proving systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community, expertise, and educational resources
rubrics_metrics.description: The Mathlib community includes leading mathematicians, computer scientists, and industry practitioners who actively contribute to and support the library. The library has also become a valuable educational resource, with courses at universities around the world using Lean and Mathlib.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the size and activity of the community, availability of experts (e.g., Zulip chat), learning materials, and university course adoption — all reduce adoption friction and provide support channels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical onboarding steps for adoption
rubrics_metrics.description: If you are considering Lean and Mathlib ... Connect with Experts: Join the Lean community's Zulip chat; Engage with Learning Materials: The Mathlib community learning page provides many excellent resources; Explore the Library: Visit the Mathlib GitHub repository; Assess Coverage: Review the Mathlib community library overview or the Mathlib documentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow concrete initial actions: contact maintainers/community, use curated learning resources, inspect the repository and documentation, and compare library coverage to project needs before committing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for strongest approaches and cohesiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Only the strongest approach to any given topic is included. Maintaining the cohesiveness of the library as a whole is a key goal of the review process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating contributions or forks, prioritize solutions aligning with the library's chosen canonical approaches to minimize fragmentation; prefer libraries that enforce cohesive design choices.
